tagline: Lake shores and river cliffs connect the Cookson Hills with Tahlequah
intro: The Cherokee Hills Byway follows lake shores, wooded Ozark foothills and the Illinois River across 84 miles of eastern Oklahoma. Oklahoma’s tourism department presents this nationally designated drive through its combination of Lake Tenkiller, the Cookson Hills, Cherokee history in Tahlequah and the river beyond. North of Tahlequah, the route parallels the Illinois, with sheer cliff faces appearing along its bends.

The lake section crosses a landscape changed by a federal water project. Between 1947 and 1952, the Army Corps of Engineers built Tenkiller’s earth-fill dam for flood control, power, water supply and recreation. The Tenkiller family, Cherokees whose name the project carries, owned land and a ferry bought for the reservoir. The original town of Cookson was among the communities flooded.

Begin on Highway 10 north of I-40 and head to Gore, then use Highways 100 and 82 past Lake Tenkiller, Cookson and Keys to Tahlequah. Tahlequah is the capital of both the Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians. Continue north beside the Illinois River on Highway 10, then turn east onto Highway 59/412-Alternate. Natural Falls lies along the northern part of the drive, before the byway ends at West Siloam Springs on the Arkansas line.

moments.title: Lake Tenkiller
moments.text: Lake Tenkiller occupies a dammed section of the Illinois River. The reservoir takes its name from the Tenkiller family, Cherokees who owned the land and ferry purchased for the project. The Army Corps of Engineers completed the earth-fill dam in 1952, with full operation beginning in 1953. The lake now occupies 12,900 acres in the Cookson Hills, with more than 130 miles of shoreline. Tenkiller State Park and Cherokee Landing State Park border its waters. The original town of Cookson is among the older communities flooded by the lake; its ruins remain beneath the water.

moments.title: Cherokee National Capitol
moments.text: Red brick and white-painted wood trim distinguish the Cherokee National Capitol on Tahlequah’s Courthouse Square. Built from 1867 to 1869 after the Civil War destroyed most of the city’s public buildings, it housed the Nation’s court, offices and tribal council meetings. Architect C. W. Goodlander gave it an Italianate design, with segmented arches over the ground-floor windows and rounded arches above. The building reopened as the Cherokee National History Museum in 2019, an art and cultural history museum. The museum’s exhibits include works by Cherokee artists and objects loaned from collections including the Cherokee Nation Archives.
moments.notice: Ground-floor windows have segmented arches; the second-floor windows have rounded arches.

moments.title: Natural Falls
moments.text: A 77-foot waterfall drops through rock formations into a narrow, V-shaped valley at Natural Falls. The property was a private highway attraction called Dripping Springs until Oklahoma bought it in 1990. Its earlier owners provided a rest stop with a swimming pool and gardens. The state chose the Natural Falls name to distinguish the park from other Oklahoma places called Dripping Springs. The park has a viewing platform above the falls and a seating deck at their base. Moist conditions support ferns, mosses and liverworts beneath forest that includes maples and white oaks.
moments.notice: Ferns, mosses and liverworts grow in the moist environment created by the falls.
